content:
If you live alone with arthritis, a falls plan means that if you do fall, someone knows quickly and can get in. Keep a way to call for help on you at all times, such as a personal alarm you can press with stiff or swollen fingers, or a mobile phone in a pocket rather than on a table. Arrange a daily check-in with someone, and make sure responders can get into your home, for example with a key safe or a trusted neighbour who has a key. Practise how you would get up from the floor while you are well, ideally with a physiotherapist. If you fall, stay calm, check for injury, and only get up if you feel able to; if not, call for help, keep warm and change position about every 30 minutes. Call 999 if you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip or cannot get up. After any fall, tell your GP, who can refer you to a falls service. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is about the plan for if you fall when nobody else is at home. For lighting and the night-time route, see night lights and safer night-time trips. For lowering your risk of falling in the first place, see the falls prevention guide.

Why living alone changes the plan

Most falls do not cause serious injury. The danger when you live alone is being on the floor for a long time, getting cold, thirsty and sore, because nobody knows. Arthritis can make getting up harder, especially with painful knees or hips, weak grip or stiff mornings. A good plan shortens the time between a fall and help arriving.

1. A way to call for help that is always on you

  • A personal alarm (pendant or wrist button) connects you to a response centre. Many councils run one, and private providers do too. There is usually a charge, so ask what is included and whether they can send a responder, not only phone a relative. See community alarms.
  • If your fingers are stiff or swollen, ask for a large, easy-press button and practise pressing it. See pendant alarms with swollen fingers.
  • Wear it all the time, including in the bathroom and at night, if it is waterproof. An alarm on the bedside table does not help in the hallway.
  • A mobile phone in a pocket or on a lanyard is better than nothing. Set up emergency contacts and learn how to call 999 without unlocking it.
  • Some alarms can detect a fall automatically. Ask the provider whether that would suit you.

2. Someone who checks in every day

Agree a simple daily check-in with a relative, friend or neighbour, such as a morning text or phone call. Agree what they will do if you do not answer, and who they will call. Some areas have telephone befriending or check-in services; Age UK and your council can tell you what is local.

3. A way for help to get in

  • A key safe outside your door lets responders or paramedics in without breaking the door. Give the code only to people who need it, such as your alarm provider.
  • Or leave a spare key with a trusted neighbour who is usually at home.
  • Keep a short note of your conditions, medicines, allergies and next of kin somewhere easy to find, such as on the fridge door.

4. Practise getting up while you are well

The NHS describes the steps: take your time, roll onto your side, get onto your hands and knees, crawl to something sturdy such as a heavy chair, put one foot flat on the floor and push up slowly, then sit and rest. With arthritis in your knees, a cushion under them can help. Practising this with a physiotherapist is the safest way to learn which version works for your joints. Leg strength work makes getting up easier too. See sit-to-stand practice.

5. If you fall and cannot get up

  • Stay calm and check yourself for pain or injury before you move.
  • Press your alarm or use your phone. If you cannot reach either, shout or bang on the wall or floor.
  • Keep warm. Pull over anything you can reach: a coat, towel, rug or blanket. Being cold for a long time can be dangerous; see the NHS page on hypothermia.
  • Keep moving gently and change position about every 30 minutes, to protect your skin.
  • If you can, shuffle towards a soft surface or a doorway where someone may see or hear you.

Some areas have a falls response service that can come out to help someone up who is not injured. See community falls response.

When to call 999, NHS 111 or your GP

  • Call 999 if you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, cannot get up, or someone is very unwell after a fall.
  • NHS 111 if you have fallen and may be in pain, injured or unwell.
  • See your GP after any fall, even a small one, or if you are worried about your balance. They can check your medicines, eyesight, blood pressure and strength, and refer you to a falls service. In some areas you can refer yourself; ask your GP surgery.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself, even if you think it is making you dizzy. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Free help with equipment and home safety

Anyone can ask their council for a free care needs assessment, which can look at alarms, grab rails, equipment and other changes to make your home safer. Apply on GOV.UK or phone your council's adult social care team. An occupational therapist may visit to look at your home.

After a fall

It is normal to feel shaken and to start avoiding things. Doing less often makes muscles weaker and the next fall more likely. See confidence after a fall, and ask about strength and balance classes.

For family and carers

If someone you love lives alone, help them choose and set up an alarm, agree a check-in routine, and sort out a key safe or spare key. Ask them gently whether they have had any near misses. People often keep small falls to themselves.

Common questions

Do I have to pay for a personal alarm?

Usually there is a weekly or monthly charge, but costs and help vary by council. Ask your council or Age UK what is available locally, and ask for a care needs assessment.

Is a smartwatch enough?

Some can detect falls and call for help, but they need charging and a signal. If you choose one, check it works in every room and that you will keep it charged and on.

Should I try to get up straight away?

No. Rest and check yourself first. Only get up if you feel able to and are not hurt. If you might have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, stay where you are and call 999.
